chapter_theme: Songs at Vallimalai (வள்ளிமலை), the hill where Murugan wooed Valli: the poet confesses the lure of women, the body as a bag of filth, sectarian wrangling and a household life that ends on the pyre, and asks for the feet before Death comes; the praise keeps returning to the hill itself, the valli creeper and the god who bowed at the hunter girl's feet.
structure_note: Every song but 538 ends on a punning refrain built from வள்ளி (the creeper, the hill, the girl): வள்ளிபடர் சாரல் வள்ளிமலை, வள்ளிக்குழாம் அடர்ந்த வள்ளிக்கல், வள்ளிக்கு வாய்த்த. 534 and 536 share the formula கள்வைத்த தோற்பை for the body. 537 is spoken for a lovesick girl, not by the poet. 538 and 539 both make Murugan the one who praises or worships Valli's feet.

530.reading: The poet tells of women whose lily eyes and jasmine smiles raise a sea of desire, and of the day when home and young kin slowly turn strangers and Yama on his strong buffalo mocks him and plunders his life; he asks for Murugan's golden anklets on that day so that he may be saved. The praise names the guru who teaches the Lord whom the ancient Vedas sought and could not find, the one who dwells in the forest that shamed the leaping spotted deer, and whose vel killed the asuras so that the gods might live, Valli's bridegroom at Vallimalai.
530.nuance: இல்லும் இளையோரும் மெல்ல அயலாக, home and the young ones slowly becoming strangers, is the dying man's isolation before Death's arrival (வல்லெருமை மாயச் சமனாரும் எள்ளி). தொல்லைமறை தேடி இல்லையெனு நாதர் is Siva, whom the Vedas sought and could not find, and Murugan is his teacher. The spotted deer shamed (புள்ளியுழை நாண) may allude to Valli's birth from a doe; that is my guess. The line அள்ளவினி தாகி நள்ளிரவு போலும் உள்ளவினை யாரத் தனமாரும் is hard to construe.

531.reading: The poet lists what holds him: phlegm and disease, infatuation, the five senses of desire, the mire of many books of stratagem he cannot cross, a heart that leaps and dies in them, the false wish for household life, a body that never turns to the yoga by which the soul is saved; he, who talks petty knowledge and suffers, asks to be joined to the two good feet. The praise names the one whose twelve red shoulders embrace the woman of the true grove, who fought Sura as the mango in the sea so that the kin of the rider of the white elephant might live, the lord of the peacock and of the three Tamils, Valli's bridegroom at Vallimalai.
531.nuance: உபாயப் பலநூலின் அள்ளல், the swamp of many books of means, sets bookish learning beside phlegm and lust as one more bondage; புல்லறிவு பேசி, 'speaking petty knowledge', is the poet's verdict on himself. The remedy named is yoga (ஆவி உய்யும்வகை யோகம்) and then the feet. வெள்ளமுது மாவை, Sura as the mango tree in the sea, is the usual battle myth; வெள்ளையிபம் ஏறு வள்ளல் is Indra on Airavata.

532.reading: The poet confesses that he left the true life for a false one, became infatuated, fell on women with hearts like stone and thieving breasts, and grew weary serving the tricks of the low and the liars; he asks Murugan to tell him the one thing by which the mind dies within and never droops again. The praise names Devayanai of the five trees of heaven, the fierce cock on his banner that crows against the night, the one who ran round the world while the father gave to the five-handed one, and the lord who climbed Valli's hill thick with creepers in longing for Valli.
532.nuance: உள்ளத்தின் மாய்வது ஒன்றை மொழியாயோ asks for a teaching that makes the mind itself die, not only for rescue; how the poet means it is my inference. வையத்தை ஓடி ஐந்து கையற்கு வீசு தந்தை points to the story of the fruit: Murugan circled the world while Siva gave the prize to Ganapati; the following words (மெய்யொத்த நீதி கண்ட) and much of the first half are hard to split.

533.reading: The poet, wilting before jasmine, Kama's bow and women's teeth and striving for pleasure, sees the end ahead, the body folding, burned in the firebrands and dropped into the pit, and asks whether he will leave the company of those who never think of Murugan's name of grace. The praise names the one who wears a garland for the creeper-like woman given by the elephant, the lord born among lotuses in the pool fed by the Ganga, the son of the destroyer of the cities at Thillai with twelve wrestling shoulders, who went up the creeper-thick hill in longing for Valli.
533.nuance: கொள்ளிக்குள் மூழ்கி வெந்து பள்ளத்தில் வீழ்வது, sinking into the pyre's brands, burning and falling into the pit, gives the end of the pleasure-seeker in one line. The middle (ஞான எல்லைக்கு மாரணங்கள் ... இணங்கை ஒழிவேனோ) is very hard to split and my reading of it is a guess. அல்லைக்கவானை தந்த வல்லி is probably Devayanai, raised by the elephant Airavata.

534.reading: The poet names his body as a string of bags: a heap-bag of deceit, a holed bag of flesh, a skin bag holding the toddy of anger, a leaking bag of wind, a bag of rubbish, a bag of the mire of soul and bond, of delusion, of pus, and a carcass for dogs to drag and tear, a body no one would take; he asks whether he will be rid of it. The praise names Murugan as nephew of Vishnu on the flood, as the one who came by the forest path loud with crickets, and as the lord destined for Valli who guarded her creeper-thick hill.
534.nuance: Every unit of the first half ends in பை, bag: குவாற்பை, புலாற்பை, தோற்பை, காற்பை, அள்ளற்பை, சீப்பை. பசுபாச அள்ளற்பை makes the body the swamp in which the soul's bond is held. Several of the bag-words (ஞெள்ளற்பை, துராற்பை) and most of the praise (வெள்ளுத்தி மால், சிள்ளிட்ட காட்டில் உள்ளக் கிரார்) are obscure to me.

535.reading: The poet, struck by Kama with his jasmine arrows, caught in a house of false talk and care, asks whether he must be tossed among the learned quarrels of the stubborn logicians of the six sects and their many paths of meaning. The praise names the younger brother whose cock crows away the night, the god of boundless compassion, the lord who grants grace and is welcomed at Vallai, Thillai and by Valli, the one destined for Valli who guarded her hill.
535.nuance: சமயமாறின் பல்லத்த மார்க்க வல்லர்க்கர் மூர்க்கர் கல்விக் கலாத்து அலையலாமோ, 'must I wander in the learned wrangling of the stubborn logicians of the six sects', is the clearest line; the rest of the song is dense rhythm and its splitting is mostly my guess.

536.reading: The poet asks not to carry the body, a thieving worm-house of flesh made of sky, wind, fire, water and earth, a skin bag holding the toddy of anger and pride; he asks to be given the inner eye that sees the one thing that remains at the end of the ages, the shining formless form the end of the Vedas speaks of. The praise names Murugan as the treasure of Siva, whom Brahma, lord of the white lady in the lotus, could not see, who bears the poison and took the many-mouthed flood on his matted hair, and as husband of the emerald Valli of the hunters' clan on the hill.
536.nuance: The plea moves from the five elements of the body (ககனம், அநிலம், அனல், புனல், நிலம்) to the one thing beyond the end of the ages (யுக இறுதிகளின் இறுதியில் ஒரு பொருள்) seen with the inner eye. அருவுரு, formless form, and மறை இறுதி, the Veda's end, are Vedantic terms. வெள்ளைப் பிராட்டி இறை is Brahma as Saraswati's lord.

537.reading: A song for a lovesick girl: bodiless Kama shoots his lily arrows, the young moon scatters fire, the south wind stirs her doubt on the bed, and the speaker asks that Murugan, without being angry at the lotus-like girl standing alone or calling it her old karma, give her his kadamba garland where the striped bees drink honey. The praise names him the poet who reached the shore of all learning, who taught the one word when Siva wearing honeyed konrai worshipped him, and the peacock hero who married Valli on Vallimalai.
537.nuance: The girl (அரவிந்த வல்லி) is spoken of, not speaking, so the voice is a mother's or friend's, and the cure asked is the god's garland, the lover's token. கொன்றை வள்ளல்தொழ அன்று கல்லறைவு ஒன்றை அருள்வோனே seems to mean teaching Siva the one word to learn, the Om story without the word Om; the split is uncertain.

538.reading: The poet confesses that he took household life, mother, wife, children, women with cuckoo voices, good family and wealth as all he needed and did not grasp the guru's word; he asks whether, before cruel Yama ends his days and he is carried off in grief and burned at the cremation ground, he will come to know Murugan's two feet. The praise names the Kumara on the spotted peacock who guards the silver mountain in the north, the good bridegroom who praised beautiful Valli's feet and guarded Vallimalai, who removes the faults of earlier days, and who is good to devotees who crown his feet with lilies.
538.nuance: The household, not the courtesan, is the snare here: குடிவாழ்க்கை அன்னை மனையாட்டி பிள்ளை, all taken as a gain (வாய்த்தது) while the குருவார்த்தை went unheard. வள்ளி அடிபோற்றி, praising Valli's feet, reverses the usual direction of worship, and 539 does the same.

539.reading: The poet describes the body as an illusion held together of head, limbs, eyes, ears, a deceitful heart, blood and bone, which has a few sorrows and joys and then burns in red fire, while the soul, crying that Death has come quickly to fight, wanders and perishes; before that he asks for a love free of karma that seeks Murugan's feet. The praise names Vishnu who sleeps on the serpent, the vel that split Sura's chest when the gods fled, and the lord who, on the hill where deer, elephants, bees and monkeys play, stood and worshipped the lotus feet of the hunter girl.
539.nuance: திண்பொருந்திடு மாயம, an illusion firmly joined, is the body; அந்தகன் பொரவந்தது, 'Death has come to fight', is the soul's cry at the end. The closing line (குறமங்கை பங்கயம் வரநின்று கும்பிடும்) has the god worship the girl's feet, the same reversal as 538.

540.reading: The poet describes lovemaking with false women, from delighting in their kohl eyes and stroking their feet to the cries of birds, falling into the pool of the navel, melting like wax in fire, biting lips, nail marks, the scattered hair and the bed, and asks whether he will ever forget that pleasure, which wipes out awareness, and think of Murugan. The praise names Rama, who crossed the sea with the monkeys, entered Lanka and cut off the demon's heads, as his uncle, and Murugan as the vel who at Madurai scattered the Jains and spread the white ash crying 'Hara Hara Sankara', son of Aram Valar Sundari, who came gladly to the woman's hill.
540.nuance: வரைவில் பொய் மங்கையர், 'false women without bounds', comes close to the classical word for courtesans (வரைவின் மகளிர்), but no money is named. மதுரையில் வெண்பொடியும் மரந்திட அரகர சங்கர என்று வென்றருள் is Sambandar's victory over the Jains, given to Murugan. அறம்வளர் சுந்தரி is the goddess Dharmasamvardhini; அரிவை விலங்கல், 'the woman's hill', is Vallimalai.

links.note: Both see the body as a bag full of holes (Naladiyar தொளைபலவாய், 534 தொள்ளைப் புலாற்பை). The Naladiyar tells the lover to look at the desired body as a bag turned inside out; 534 turns the image on the poet's own body and asks to be rid of it.
Both take the poet's body apart as a list of containers, pot, bellows and bag in 280, a dozen kinds of bag in 534, and both ask for the end of that body rather than its health.
Both songs call the body கள்வைத்த தோற்பை, a skin bag holding toddy, a formula the poet reuses. In 534 it is one of a dozen bags; 536 sets it against the formless form seen by the inner eye.

Both set the sect-disputers' learning aside: 124 opens with sectarians who cannot see one another's truth, 535 asks not to be tossed in the wrangling of the six sects' logicians. 535's reading rests on one clear line in a dense song.
Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, tormented by the moon and the breeze, and ask him for his garland as the cure; 537 adds a plea that he not blame her old karma.

530 sees home and the young ones slowly becoming strangers (இல்லும் இளையோரும் மெல்ல அயலாக) as Yama on his buffalo comes to take his life. Tirumanthiram 157 has the wailing kin, wives and children turn back at the town's edge (ஊர்த்துறைக் காலே ஒழிவர்). Both show the family stopping short of the dying man's road.

531 counts the swamp of many books of means (உபாயப் பலநூலின் அள்ளல்) among his bonds and names yoga as the way the soul is saved. 709, in a distant chapter, sets the read books and argued creeds (வாசித்த நூல் மதங்கள்) against the bindu-light and yogic samadhi. Both place learning on the side of bondage and yoga on the side of release.

532 asks Murugan to tell the one thing by which the mind dies within (உள்ளத்தின் மாய்வது ஒன்றை மொழியாயோ) and never droops again; the reading of the uncertain line is the link's basis. Tirumanthiram 2956 says that when the mind's maya itself dies (மனமாயை தான்மாய) nothing else remains to die. Tirumular states as doctrine what the song only asks for.

533 begins wilting before jasmine (முல்லை) and women's teeth (பல்லுக்கும் வாடி) and ends with the body burned in the brands and dropped in the pit. Naladiyar 45 refuses the men who call smiles jasmine buds and sets against them teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground (புறங்காட்டு உதிர்ந்துக்க பல்லென்பு). The same jasmine-teeth figure leads both to the cremation ground, in the Naladiyar as the cure for desire, in the song as its end.

535 asks whether he must wander in the learned wrangling of the stubborn logicians of the six sects (சமயமாறின் ... வல்லர்க்கர் மூர்க்கர் கல்விக் கலாத்து). Tirumanthiram 1558 says the six sects are six roads to one city and those who argue 'this is good, that bad' are dogs barking at a hill. Both treat the sectarian quarrel itself as the fault.

536 asks for the knowledge that sees with the inner eye (உள்ளக்கண் நோக்கும் அறிவு) the one thing at the end of the ages, after refusing the body of five elements. Tirumanthiram 2944 says fools see with the eyes in their faces, and seeing with the eye within (அகத்திற் கண்கொண்டு) is bliss. Both make the inner eye the organ of the real.

537 praises Murugan as the poet who reached the shore of all learning (கல்விகரை கண்ட புலவோனே). Naladiyar 135 says learning has no shore (கல்வி கரையில) and a short life must choose what to learn. Read literally, the song claims for the god a shore the Naladiyar denies exists for the learner; the conflict holds only if the god is measured by the human limit.

538 took mother, wife, children, family and wealth as all that was needed (குலம்வாய்த்த நல்ல தனம்வாய்த்தது) until Yama comes and he is burned at the இடுகாடு. Naladiyar 25 has the man who sees corpses carried yet marries and says 'there is, there is' (உண்டு உண்டு உண்டு) answered by the funeral drum. Both set household gain against the burning ground.

539 ends with the god who stood and worshipped the hunter girl's lotus feet (குறமங்கை பங்கயம் வரநின்று கும்பிடும்). 209, at Swamimalai, has him bow his cool crown daily on her golden feet (பொன்னடிமீது நித்தமும் தண்முடி). The reversal of worship, god to devotee, recurs far apart in the book.

540 opens with வரைவில் பொய் மங்கையர், false women without bounds, and describes their embrace. Kural 919 calls the shoulders of women who draw no line (வரைவிலா மாணிழையார்) the hell in which base men sink. The song's word is the Kural's chapter word, though the song names no price.

source_issues: Song 532: the first half (கையொத்து வாழு மிந்த ... உள்ளப்பெ றாக நின்று) is hard to split and may be corrupt.
Song 534: several bag-words (ஞெள்ளற்பை, துராற்பை, வெள்ளிட்ட சாப்பி சிதமீரல்) are unclear and may be corrupt.
